strategies.doc: Long when fast SMA is above slow SMA, short otherwise.
strategies.hypothesis: Trend persistence from slow information diffusion and from hedgers who trade on schedule rather than on price. Counterparties: forced rebalancers and risk-averse holders trimming winners. Weak but durable; expect low Sharpe and long flat periods.

strategies.doc: Long if trailing return over `lookback` is positive. Day 28 baseline.
strategies.hypothesis: Under-reaction to information plus flows that chase performance. Documented across asset classes since the 1990s, which also means it is heavily traded and its Sharpe has compressed. Test net of costs.

Liquidity provision: you are paid for absorbing impatient order flow. Counterparty is someone who needs to trade now. Fails catastrophically when the move is information-driven rather than liquidity-driven -- which is why this needs a stop, always.

models.title: Statistical arbitrage
models.question: DOES IT REVERT?
models.sub: pairs, and whether the spread comes back
models.blurb: Fits a hedge ratio, tests the spread for stationarity against the critical value for a *fitted* relationship, and measures how long a shock takes to decay. A spread that reverts too slowly to trade is not a pair, and screening sixty of them and keeping the best is not a discovery. Both facts are reported next to the Sharpe.

params.help: pair: two prices tied together by an OU spread with a known half-life — the positive control. panel: a cross-section with no planted relationship, screened pair by pair.
Bars to generate.
Same seed, same data. Change it and see whether the answer survives.
Names in the panel (source=panel). Screening C(n,2) pairs is the multiple-comparisons tax, so this number sets the bill.
Planted half-life in bars (source=pair). The model should recover roughly this number.
Planted hedge ratio (source=pair).
Trailing window for the z-score, and the holding window the half-life is judged against.
Enter when |z| exceeds this, fading the move.
Exit when |z| falls inside this. Must be below entry_z.
Estimate the hedge ratio on trailing data only. Turn it off and every signal knows its own future — kept because seeing the gap is instructive, not because the number is real.
Which cost model the pair's P&L is charged.

rules.message: entry_z must be greater than exit_z, otherwise the bands cross
{n} bars against {warmup} bars of warmup leaves no sample to judge; use at least {min_n} bars or a shorter z_window

models.title: Factor investing
models.question: WHAT IS IT EXPOSED TO?
models.blurb: Scores every name on price-only factors, sorts the cross-section into quantiles and grades the sort. Whether the quantiles line up in order matters more than the top-minus-bottom number, and which leg the money came from decides whether you could have put the trade on at all.

params.help: Names in the universe.
Bars to generate.
Same seed, same data. Change it and see whether the answer survives.
Annualised drift planted in proportion to factor-1 beta. Zero is the null: an IC interval that excludes zero on this data is a bug in the pipeline, not a factor.
Buckets to sort into. Cannot exceed n_assets.
Bars between rebalances, and the bootstrap block length.

Averaged with EQUAL weights, so factors that disagree cancel: momentum and reversal are opposite signs of the same number, and selecting both is close to selecting neither. Fitting the weights on this same sample is the easiest way to manufacture an IC, so they are not fitted.
Cost model for the long-short book.

rules.message: {n_assets} assets cannot be split into {n_quantiles} quantiles; use fewer buckets or a wider universe
{factors} needs {needed} bars of warmup plus one {rebalance}-bar holding period; ask for at least {min_n} bars

models.title: Value at Risk
models.question: WHAT COULD IT LOSE?
models.sub: three methods, and whether they agree
models.blurb: Historical, Gaussian and Cornish-Fisher on the same returns, side by side, then a trailing-window backtest that counts how often the estimate was wrong and whether the misses arrived together. When three defensible methods disagree by forty percent, that spread is the result.

params.help: synthetic: one price path. panel-asset: the first name out of an eight-name cross-section, so its risk carries factor structure.
Bars to generate.
Same seed, same data. Change it and see whether the answer survives.
Draw shocks from a Student-t instead of a normal. The three methods agree on Gaussian data; this is where they stop.
The level the estimate claims. Higher needs a longer window.
Bars ahead, scaled by sqrt(h) — which assumes returns are independent, and they are least independent when this matters.
Trailing window for the rolling VaR that gets backtested.

rules.message: a {window}-bar window holds no observation beyond the {alpha} quantile; at {confidence} confidence you need at least {min_window} bars of window
{n} bars leaves nothing to backtest a {window}-bar window against; ask for at least {min_n}

models.title: Machine learning
models.question: DID IT LEARN, OR MEMORISE?
models.blurb: A ridge regression from price features to the next bar's return, walked forward, with the standardisation fitted on the training fold only. The gap between train IC and test IC is the headline, and the bar the model has to clear is the best single feature — one line of code.

params.help: Bars to generate.
Same seed, same data. Change it and see whether the answer survives.
Bars in each training fold.
Bars in each test fold.
Ridge penalty, on the un-normalised scale — the same alpha is a strong penalty on 100 rows and almost none on 5000.
All six are functions of the same price path, so the coefficients are collinear and will swing sign between folds.

rules.message: one {train}+{test} fold plus {warmup} bars of feature warmup needs {needed} bars; you asked for {n}

models.title: Portfolio optimisation
models.question: HOW SHOULD IT BE WEIGHTED?
models.sub: the frontier is a band, not a line
models.blurb: Mean-variance weights, then the same optimisation run again on bootstrap resamples of the same data. If a different draw of the same market would have told you to hold a different book, the first book was never knowledge. Equal weight and inverse vol are the benchmarks, and they are free to estimate.

params.help: Assets to allocate between.
Bars to generate.
Same seed, same data. Change it and see whether the answer survives.
Plants drift in proportion to factor-1 beta, so there is something real for the optimiser to find. Zero is the null.
Points on the frontier.
Bootstrap draws. The band is the deliverable, so this is the one number worth spending time on.
Constrain to w >= 0, sum w = 1. Allow shorting and the instability figure stops being bounded, or comparable.
Shrinkage toward constant correlation. Leave empty for the Ledoit-Wolf estimate.

rules.message: {n} bars cannot estimate a covariance matrix for {n_assets} assets

models.title: Time-series momentum
models.question: DOES THE TREND PERSIST?
models.sub: and does it still pay one knob either side
models.blurb: Buys what went up and sells what went down, then sweeps the lookback from 5 to 250 bars and reports the Sharpe against it with an interval on every point. The headline is not the deliverable — the decay curve is. A strategy that works at exactly 30 bars and dies at 25 and 35 is a peak between two holes, and the sweep taxes itself for having looked.

params.help: Bars to generate — a price path with no edge in it, so the honest answer is known before the sweep starts.
Same seed, same data. Change it and see whether the answer survives.
Bars of trailing return the sign is taken from. This is the one knob everybody has turned until it paid, which is why the neighbouring settings are reported next to it.
Bars a position is held, as overlapping books rather than a rebalance grid — so the answer does not depend on which day of the month you happened to start.

Bars between the end of the lookback and the trade. The classic construction skips the last month because the most recent bars reverse; zero is the honest default for a time-series signal and does leave that reversal inside it.

Run the lookback and holding sweeps and the walk-forward. Turn it off and n_trials becomes 1, which is a claim that exactly one hypothesis was tested — rarely true of anyone who already chose a number.
Cost model the turnover is charged at. Momentum's edge is small and its turnover is not, so this knob moves the answer.

rules.message: {n} bars against a {lookback}-bar lookback, a {holding}-bar hold and a {skip}-bar skip leaves {tradable} bars to trade; {min_grade} is the fewest this module will grade, so ask for at least {min_n} bars

models.title: Monte Carlo
models.question: WHAT DOES THE TAIL LOOK LIKE?
models.sub: resampled futures against the normal fit
models.blurb: Resamples the observed bars into thousands of futures and prices the assumption you avoided: the same simulation is run again from a fitted normal, and the gap between the two 1st percentiles is the headline. Every path inherits the drift of the sample it was drawn from, so the median is the past re-expressed, never a forecast.

params.help: Bars of history to resample FROM. No resampling can produce a crash the sample has never seen, so this is the ceiling on how bad the simulated tail is allowed to be.
Same seed, same data. Change it and see whether the answer survives.
Futures to draw. Below a hundred there is no 1st percentile to read; the interval on the tail gap narrows with this number and with nothing else.
Bars forward. Summing bars pulls the distribution toward a normal whatever the bars look like, which is why a fitted normal is least wrong at exactly the horizon people quote it over.

block_bootstrap keeps runs of bad days together. bootstrap breaks them up. gaussian is the null this panel exists to argue with — it cannot surprise the normal fit it is compared against, and the verdict says so.
Bars per block (method=block_bootstrap). This is the whole point of the method: volatility clusters, and drawing bars independently destroys the clustering that makes tails deep.
Drawdown depth counted as ruin. P(touching it) is reported with its own binomial standard error, because a probability off 2000 paths is itself an estimate.

rules.message: a {block}-bar block cannot be resampled into a {horizon}-bar path; use a block shorter than the horizon

models.title: Option pricing
models.question: WHAT IS THIS CONTRACT WORTH?
models.sub: Black-Scholes, and what it assumes away
models.blurb: Prices one European option, differentiates it, and audits itself against put-call parity — which must close to floating-point noise or the pricer has a bug and nothing else on the panel should be read. Supply a market price and it solves for the volatility that reproduces it. Nothing here is estimated from data and nothing carries an interval: the only uncertainty in the number is the volatility, and that is an input.

params.help: Price of the underlying today.
Exercise price. At the money is where the time value is largest and where the greeks are most sensitive to the volatility.
Continuously compounded risk-free rate. Negative is allowed because it has happened.
Annualised volatility, assumed constant to expiry — which it will not be. This single number is the entire model.
Years to expiry, and at least one day of it. At zero the option is its intrinsic value and the greeks divide by nothing.
Call or put. Parity ties the two together, and the audit checks that it does.

A quote to solve for implied volatility against. Leave it EMPTY to skip the solve — empty means 'do not ask', and it is not the same as a quote of zero, which is a claim that the contract is worthless and would imply a volatility of nothing.

rules.message: tau is {tau} years: an option with no time left to run is worth its intrinsic value, and its greeks are dividing by zero
vol is {vol}: a price computed at zero volatility is a discounted certainty, not an option

models.title: Volatility targeting
models.question: WHAT DOES CONSTANT RISK COST?
models.sub: against a book holding the same risk
models.blurb: Scales a buy-and-hold position by trailing volatility to hold risk constant, and bills it for the turnover that takes. The comparison that matters is not against the untargeted book — most of that gap is simply holding less — but against a constant-leverage book carrying the same full-sample volatility. The protection also arrives late, and the lag is measured rather than assumed.

params.help: Bars to generate. Two books and a fold split need history.
Same seed, same data. Change it and see whether the answer survives.
Annualised volatility the rule aims at. Aim well below the asset's own and the book spends its life at the leverage cap, targeting nothing.
Trailing bars the volatility estimate is built from. Short reacts sooner and wobbles more; the tracking error has a floor set by this number that no rule can beat.
Cap on gross position. Bars where it binds are bars where the rule stopped targeting anything, and the fraction is reported.
Cost model the extra turnover is charged at. This is the fee side of the whole trade-off.

rules.message: {n} bars cannot carry a {window}-bar volatility estimate and still split two books into folds; ask for at least {min_n} bars

tape.title: The Opening Tape
tape.question: WHAT DOES EVERY MODEL SAY ABOUT THIS NAME?
tape.sub: one ticker, nine models, one grade
tape.blurb: Runs every model this repo owns over one real ticker in a single pass and grades the result on how many independent intervals cleared zero — not on how good the best one looked. On real single-name daily data the answer is C almost every time, and that is the grading working rather than the name failing.

params.help: A real symbol. Prices come from Yahoo via jamiequant.data.market, which raises rather than inventing a series when it cannot fetch one.
Trailing window. The standard error of an annualised Sharpe is sqrt(252/n_bars): 1.00 at one year, 0.58 at three. History is fetched from 2015-01-01, so asking for more than that returns what exists.

Fetch Form 4 disclosures from SEC EDGAR. Needs a User-Agent (HEYJAMIE_SEC_UA); without one the block comes back None, which means 'not fetched' and never 'nobody is trading'. This is the slowest single step.
The cross-section for the pair, factor and optimiser sections, up to 30 names. Empty means the eleven SPDR sector ETFs, which stand in for the sector and are not this issuer's competitors.

tape.title: Universe screen
tape.question: IS THE BEST NAME BETTER THAN THE BEST COIN FLIP?
tape.sub: ranked, and charged for the ranking
tape.blurb: Ranks a universe on risk-adjusted return and then draws the line where luck alone would have reached for a search of that size. Measured on this desk: the best real one-year Sharpe among 40 liquid names was 2.50, and screening 100 zero-edge series hands you 2.53 for free. The line is the only thing on the leaderboard that was compared against anything.

params.help: Today's index members, which is why every result here is survivorship-biased upward.
Window and thresholds. 'extreme' is the original ask and returns nothing: 0 of 40 liquid names pass it on either window.
Rows to show. Never padded — if eleven names pass you get eleven rows.
Overrides the preset's window. Empty keeps it.
Overrides the preset's return bar. A threshold someone chose is not evidence; the luck line is.
Overrides the preset's drawdown cap, as a POSITIVE magnitude: 0.25 means 'no worse than -25%'.

presets.note: Default. 3-year window, roughly the p75 of liquid US names (measured: median Sharpe 0.86, median max drawdown -23.6%). Passing this is ordinary, not exceptional.
Prop-desk drawdown cap. The return bar is unchanged from 'institutional'; the 10% drawdown limit is what makes it bite, and it mostly selects for low volatility rather than for skill.

1-year window. The standard error of an annualised Sharpe over 1 year is 1.00, so a 1.50 here and a 0.50 here are two draws that routinely swap places. Expect this preset to pass names that will not repeat.

The original request. Measured: 0 of the 40 most liquid US names pass this on a 1-year window, and 0 of 40 on a 3-year window. It is kept so the ask can be run and shown to be empty rather than quietly softened.

params.help: 2 to 12 rows of {symbol, asset_class, weight}. The class is not cosmetic: it decides which cost schedule the line is charged, and on the shipped config that is 18.0 bps a turn for crypto against 4.0 for equity and an ETF and 2.0 for FX. `weight` is null unless allocation is 'custom'.

How the weights are decided. The four estimated methods (inverse_vol, risk_parity, max_sharpe, min_variance) solve on a trailing window and are the ones graded hardest, because beating equal weight is their entire claim. 'buy_and_hold' is a benchmark, not a strategy.
When the book is traded back to target. 'none' still buys the allocation once, on the first bar it exists, and charges that purchase — it does not mean the allocation is never held.
Bars between rebalances. 21 is monthly on a daily calendar. Ignored unless rebalance is 'periodic'.

Trade when any weight is this far from its target. 0.05 is five percentage points. Ignored unless rebalance is 'drift_band'. A band the book never reaches makes this a buy-and-hold run, and the payload carries a warning saying so.

First bar. The panel is trimmed to the span every symbol actually printed in, so one young name shortens the whole book; per_symbol in the calendar block says which. Fewer than 60 aligned bars is refused rather than measured.

'intersection' keeps only days every symbol traded — it throws history away and invents nothing. 'union_ffill' keeps the union and carries the last price forward, which invents zero-return bars: measured, forward-filling BTC onto SPY's calendar moved their correlation from +0.423 to +0.392, downward, which flatters diversification. The engine calls this one 'forward_fill'.

rules.message: a portfolio needs at least 2 holdings; you gave {n_holdings}. One name has no correlation, no diversification ratio and no risk to decompose — run it on the backtest panel, which answers that question properly.
this desk runs at most 12 holdings; you gave {n_holdings}. A wider book is a longer fetch and a correlation matrix nobody can read, not a better answer.
{n_duplicate_symbols} symbol(s) appear on more than one row. Combine them into one line: two rows of the same name are one position, and the allocator would solve for both of them.

{n_unknown_classes} holding(s) carry an asset_class that is not one of equity, etf, crypto, fx. The class decides which cost schedule the line is charged — 18.0 bps a turn for crypto against 4.0 for equity on the shipped config — so it cannot be guessed.

allocation='custom' means you are choosing the weights, and {n_unweighted} holding(s) carry none. The engine would split whatever is left between them, which is a different book from the one you typed.
{n_nonfinite_weights} custom weight(s) are not finite numbers. NaN and infinity are refusals here, never zeros.

a custom weight of {min_weight} is a short position. This form is long-only: the picker has no borrow control and the panel has nowhere to show one, so a negative weight would be charged and drawn as though it were a purchase.

custom weights sum to {weight_total}; they must sum to more than 0 and at most 1. Less than 1 is allowed and is not an error — the engine does NOT renormalise, so 0.8 means 20% in cash and `invested_fraction` will say so. More than 1 is leverage, which this form does not offer.

derived.help: how many rows the picker has
how many symbols appear on more than one row, counted once each
rows whose asset_class is not one of equity, etf, crypto, fx
rows carrying no weight, or a blank one
rows whose weight is not a finite number (NaN, infinity, text)
the sum of the finite weights, unnormalised
the smallest finite weight, or null if there is none

advisories.message: rebalance='none' with an estimated allocation buys the weights ONCE, on the first bar the estimator has actually solved something, and holds them from there. That purchase is charged as a trade but is not counted as a rebalance, so the result reports zero of them. It is a real run of the allocation, not equal weight under its name — but every number in it describes weights chosen on one window years ago.
allocation='buy_and_hold' overrides the rebalance schedule: a buy-and-hold book that is rebalanced is not a buy-and-hold book. The engine forces rebalance='none' and says so in `warnings`.

union_ffill keeps every symbol's calendar and carries the last known price across the gaps, which invents zero-return bars. Measured: forward-filling BTC onto SPY's calendar moved their correlation from +0.423 to +0.392 — downward, which flatters diversification. `calendar.fabricated_bars` counts them.

portfolio.title: The whole book
portfolio.question: WHAT IS THE WHOLE BOOK DOING?
portfolio.sub: several assets, one calendar, one bill
portfolio.blurb: Puts two to twelve names across four asset classes on one calendar, allocates between them, rebalances on a schedule, and charges every trade its own class's costs. Then it runs equal weight and buy-and-hold over the identical bars and grades the allocation against them rather than against zero, because the question a portfolio has to answer is not 'did it make money' but 'did it beat splitting the money evenly and going away'. Measured on a real five-asset four-class basket from 2022: two of the four estimated methods did not, and both of those are graded a fault here however much money they made.

governance_gates: 90+ consecutive days of paper trading logged
live Sharpe within 1.0 of the backtest Sharpe
live slippage within 1.5x of the modelled cost
holdout opened exactly once, on day 44, and recorded
written post-mortem for every kill-switch event
maximum acceptable loss written down and accepted in advance
